turns.input: Begin the story.
turns.output:
The upstairs room has the clean, temporary look of a place made ready for someone whose name was not known until recently: narrow bed, small wardrobe, desk beneath the window. Your luggage waits where it was brought in. Beyond the glass, Harbour Street slopes toward a strip of pale water, fishing boats reduced by distance to dark marks against the evening.

On the desk, the welcome sheet sits beside the lamp.

**Supper, 18:30 — foyer tables**  
**Induction, 09:00 tomorrow — office**  
**Staff staircase beside office**

Nell’s mobile number is printed underneath in careful block type.

Below, crockery touches crockery. A door swings shut, followed by a man’s voice carrying up from the foyer—too indistinct to make out—then a brief burst of laughter. From farther overhead comes a softer mechanical clatter, as if someone is working with a case of tools.

The coat’s mended cuff catches faintly against the desk edge when you stand near it. Downstairs, someone says, “Not that stack, those are programmes,” and another voice answers, “I know what programmes look like.”

At the bottom of the stairs, warm light reaches across the landing floorboards.

turns.input: I go down to the staff supper, introduce myself as Rowan, and take an available place.
turns.output:
You follow the staircase down into the foyer, where the last of the daylight still reaches through the glazed doors.

Two square café tables have been pushed together beneath the old film posters. A woman with a dark braid and a pencil tucked behind one ear is straightening a stack of folded opening programmes; beside her, an older man in a navy work shirt is examining the leg of a chair as if it has personally offended him. Bea Finch sits with both hands around a mug, watching the room with an alert, patient expression.

Nell comes out of the office with a clipboard under one arm. “Rowan. Good—you found us.”

You introduce yourself, and she gestures around the tables.

“Rosa Chen, who’s making the reopening exhibition. Martin Vale, who knows where every loose screw in this building has been since 1982. Bea Finch, our treasurer.”

“Former usher,” Bea adds. “Welcome.”

Martin rises enough to offer a hand. “Archive tomorrow, is it? You’ll want a decent pencil. Half the ones people leave lying about here are fit only for stirring paint.”

Rosa smiles. “Ignore him about the pencil. He’s right about most other things, unfortunately.”

From the kitchen doorway, a tall man in a rolled-sleeve shirt carries out a bowl of green salad. “Owen,” he says. “There’s a clear chair there, if you want it.”

A woman behind him sets a pie dish on the counter with a pair of oven gloves. “Jo. You’re not contributing tonight,” she says. “First supper’s on me. After that, you’ll find we all become extremely interested in receipts.”

Nell gives Jo a look that is more fond than reproachful. “Rowan’s the cataloguer for six weeks, not a new source of free labour.”

“Good. We’re already overstocked.”

You take the open chair between Owen and Bea. The food begins arriving: tomato-and-chickpea stew in a broad blue pot, the cheese-and-onion pie with its browned crust cut into uneven wedges, bread wrapped in a tea towel. For a few minutes, the table is occupied by plates, serving spoons, and the small practical negotiations of people finding room for one another.

Footsteps sound on the staff stairs. A man with a compact black equipment case comes down, pauses at the sight of the laid table, and puts it carefully beside the office door.

“Sorry,” he says. “The booth decided it wanted to be mysterious.”

“This is Dev,” Nell says. “Dev Malik, projection and sound.”

Dev pulls out the remaining chair. “And you’re Rowan. Welcome to the glamorous end of cinema.”

Martin points his fork toward the ceiling. “He means cables.”

“I mean exactly cables.”

Jo passes Dev a plate before he can reach for one. “Eat first. Be mysterious later.”

Conversation settles around the meal. Rosa tells Bea that the printer wants the exhibition layout by Wednesday, and Bea says she will bring the old usher photographs another day, “once I’ve worked out what belongs in public and what doesn’t.” Martin begins to object, then thinks better of it and tears off a piece of bread instead.

Rosa turns toward you, her pencil still tucked behind her ear.

“So—have you worked with old paper archives before?”

turns.input: I ask Nell what my first day of archive work will involve.
turns.output:
Rosa lets her question rest as you turn to Nell and ask about the morning.

Nell sets down her fork. “At nine, we’ll go through the archive workroom and the records system. The first job is knowing what we have, where it came from, and what we’re allowed to do with it.”

She gestures lightly toward the stairwell. “You’ll start with the trust’s business papers and programme boxes. They’re comparatively straightforward. For each item or group: description, date if we can establish it, condition, provenance, and whether it belongs to the trust or is on loan. If something’s fragile, unclear, or has restrictions attached, you flag it rather than trying to solve it alone.”

“So,” Bea says, “don’t let Martin persuade you that a photograph is definitely from 1987 because he remembers the weather.”

“I do remember the weather,” Martin says.

Rosa breaks a piece of bread in half. “You give all your dates weather. That’s not the same thing.”

Nell’s mouth shifts briefly toward a smile. “There are loan records to read before you handle any of those boxes. Some people are happy for material to be described but not copied or displayed. The paperwork matters as much as the object.”

She lifts her water glass. “By the end of tomorrow, I’d like you comfortable enough to make a proper start. Not to have conquered the whole building.”

Dev’s phone vibrates against the table. He glances at the screen, then looks up. “Nell—before I forget. Hana can help with the hearing-assistance test from seven. Could I have the auditorium from five past?”

Nell’s expression changes as she reaches for the clipboard beside her chair. “Rosa and Martin have it from seven until twenty to eight.”

Dev looks toward the auditorium doors. “For what?”

“The programme boards,” Rosa says. “Photographs and Martin’s notes on who painted them. It was booked on Friday.”

“I didn’t know,” Dev says at once. “I should’ve checked.”

“I could do it later,” Rosa says, though she does not sound pleased by the idea.

“No,” Nell says. “Your booking stands. Dev, don’t bring Hana in for a test that can’t happen. Ask when she’s next free and send it to me; I’ll put it in the diary properly.”

For a moment, Dev studies his phone. Then he nods. “All right.”

He steps away from the table to make the call, leaving his plate untouched beside the stew.

turns.input: I help myself to food and listen to the conversation around the table.
turns.output:
You serve yourself stew, pie, bread, and a spoonful of salad. The stew is thick with chickpeas and softened onion; steam fogs the inside of the blue pot’s lid where Jo has set it aside.

At the office doorway, Dev speaks quietly into his phone.

“No—sorry. I should’ve checked before I called you. Don’t make the trip for this. I’ll send you a proper time when we’ve got one.”

He listens for a moment, thanks Hana, and comes back to the table, slipping the phone into his pocket.

“She’s not coming in,” he says. “She’s at a hotel after half seven. I’ve asked her to send over her next free evenings.”

Nell nods. “Thank you. I’ll put an actual slot in the diary.”

“I should’ve looked in it first,” Dev says. “That’s mine.”

Rosa gives a short nod across the table. “Thanks.”

Jo points her serving spoon at Dev’s plate. “Then you can eat before the pie turns into building material.”

The conversation shifts back to the exhibition. Rosa unfolds a sheet of notes beside her glass.

“The boards are all ready where we left them,” she says to Martin. “I’ll take the photographs first, then I need you talking me through the changes. Names where you know them, dates only where you’re sure.”

Martin chews, considering this as seriously as if it were a mechanical specification. “The blue one was definitely Rafi Bell’s lettering. He used that little brush with the split ferrule. Could get a line narrow as thread out of it.”

“And the dates?” Rosa asks.

“I’ll tell you when I’m guessing.”

“That’ll do.”

Bea looks from one to the other. “It matters. People did that work here for years, and most of it went up for a week, then got painted over.”

Nell says, “That’s part of why Rowan’s records need sources as well as descriptions. A note can say Martin remembers it; it doesn’t have to pretend it came stamped with a date.”

Martin glances toward you. “Fair system, that.”

Owen has been cutting his pie into neat pieces. “Do you want me nearby when you’re moving the boards back afterward?”

“We’re only taking pictures,” Rosa says. “But maybe at twenty to eight, if you’re still about.”

“Fine by me.”

Jo shakes her head, though there is no real objection in it. “You lot are incapable of eating without arranging furniture around one another.”

“Cinema work,” Martin says. “It gets in your blood.”

“Most things get in your blood if you spend enough years not washing properly,” Bea says.

That earns a laugh from Owen and Rosa. Martin accepts it with a look of grave injury and reaches for more bread.

As the clock above the café counter approaches seven, the meal loosens into smaller exchanges: Jo asking Bea whether the new crockery has been counted; Nell making a note against the opening-weekend rota; Dev describing, in less technical language than before, the small receivers he needs to test. He leaves the equipment case by the office door for now.

Rosa gathers her camera bag and notebook. Martin takes up a pencil and a folded list of board titles. Together they cross the foyer to the auditorium doors, with Bea following far enough to hold one open while they take the first board inside.

“No sound through there for forty minutes,” Rosa calls back lightly.

“None,” Nell says.

The doors close behind them. In the foyer, Jo begins stacking plates, Owen carries the empty stew pot toward the kitchen, and Dev picks up his case for the stairs.

turns.input: I ask the person who has been working upstairs what they are working on this evening.
turns.output:
Dev pauses with the equipment case in hand.

“The hearing-assistance kit,” he says. “The new receivers turned up early, so I was getting them charged, labelled, and talking to the booth equipment. Quiet work, mostly.”

He nods toward the auditorium doors, where Rosa and Martin are now at work among the boards.

“The useful bit needs the room: one person sends test audio, another walks the seats and checks what comes through. Hana was going to help, but I hadn’t checked the diary. That part waits until Nell finds us a slot.”

Nell glances up from the rota sheet. “I will find one.”

“I know,” Dev says. “I’m not trying to turn this into an emergency.” He shifts the case against his leg. “There’s still plenty I can finish upstairs without making a noise.”

From behind the auditorium doors comes the faint scrape of a board being adjusted against the side wall, followed by Rosa’s voice, too muffled to make out.

Dev looks toward the stairs. “Anyway. That’s the glamorous answer. Batteries, settings, and me discovering which cable I’ve put in the wrong pocket.”

turns.input: I finish my supper and listen while the others make their plans.
turns.output:
You finish what is on your plate as Jo begins collecting dishes.

“Leave that,” she says, reaching for your plate. “First evening, you’re exempt from washing up.”

Dev rests a hand on his equipment case. “I’ll finish the booth setup and label the receivers. No sound, no auditorium. When Hana sends her availability, I’ll forward it to Nell before we arrange anything.”

“That’s the order of it,” Nell says. She turns her clipboard around and scans the rota notes. “And if anyone has an opening-weekend change I don’t know about, send it tomorrow. I’m finishing the rota on Wednesday.”

“I’ll check mine tonight,” Owen says.

Jo carries the stew pot back into the kitchen. “I’ll send over the last menu costs once I’ve checked the supplier invoice. My Friday van route stays where it is.”

“Fine,” Nell says. “That’s enough for now.”

A faint scrape comes through the closed auditorium doors: one of the old boards being shifted away from the side wall. Then the small, sharp click of Rosa’s camera. No test audio follows.

Owen glances at the clock above the counter. “I’ll come back at twenty to eight and help put the boards back.”

Martin’s voice carries only as an indistinct murmur from beyond the doors. Bea listens for a moment, then gathers her mug.

Dev lifts his case and heads for the staircase. Nell takes the clipboard into the office, still making notes. Jo runs water in the kitchen sink.

The foyer settles around you: the smell of onion pie, stacks of unopened crockery, evening light thinning beyond the front doors, and the quiet work of a building preparing to become public again.

turns.input: I offer to carry the empty plates back to the kitchen, without offering to take over anybody's work.
turns.output:
You offer Jo the empty plates.

She looks over from the sink, takes in the stack, and nods. “Yes, please. Draining board beside me. Don’t wash them—I haven’t decided where anything lives yet.”

You carry the plates through to the narrow kitchen. Owen shifts aside with the stew pot under one arm, leaving room at the counter. Jo points out the glasses separately and keeps the larger pans for herself.

From the auditorium comes the soft shutter-click of Rosa’s camera, then Martin’s voice through the doors: “Rafi painted that lettering. Date, I’m less certain about.”

“No problem,” Rosa answers. “I’ll mark it as your recollection.”

You set the last plate beside the sink. Beyond the kitchen doorway, the foyer has settled into its separate evening work: Nell’s pencil moving over the rota in the office, Dev’s case carried upstairs, and the old cinema boards being photographed where they stand along the auditorium’s side wall.

turns.input: If the conversation turns into an argument about who gets to use a room, I listen without deciding for them. I finish clearing away my own things.
turns.output:
You collect your glass, cutlery, and the folded napkin from your place, carrying them into the kitchen.

Jo has claimed the sink and the larger pans. She points you toward the draining board without looking up. “Those can go there. Thanks.”

You set them down and leave the kitchen clear for her work.

No dispute rises from the foyer. Upstairs, a few careful clicks and the muted close of the projection-booth door suggest Dev settling back to his equipment. Behind the auditorium doors, Rosa’s camera shutter sounds at intervals while Martin’s voice alternates between firm recollection and more cautious guesses.

At the tables, Owen gathers the abandoned bread basket and checks the clock: still some time before he has promised to help return the boards to their place along the auditorium wall.

turns.input: I go back to my room and read for twenty minutes, leaving the staff to their own projects.
turns.output:
You return upstairs, close the room door, and read at the small desk for twenty minutes.

The remaining daylight fades from Harbour Street. Now and then, a muted sound travels through the building: a camera shutter from below, footsteps on the landing, the faint clink of dishes being stacked in the kitchen. Otherwise, the cinema keeps its separate evening work to itself.

When you look up again, the desk lamp has become the brightest thing in the room.

turns.input: In private, I consider calling a future short story 'The Red Umbrella'. It is only a possible title: I have not written a story or mentioned the idea to anyone. Then I carry on reading.
turns.output:
“The Red Umbrella” passes through your mind as a possible title—nothing more, unspoken and unwritten.

You turn back to your reading beneath the desk lamp while the Picture House carries on quietly around you.

turns.input: I go downstairs for a glass of water and linger in the foyer for a few minutes.
turns.output:
Downstairs, the foyer is quieter than it was at supper. You fill a glass at the kitchen tap; Jo is still at the sink, working through the last of the pans.

In the auditorium, Rosa’s camera shutter clicks at measured intervals. Martin’s voice reaches the foyer only in fragments, lower now, as he distinguishes what he knows from what he is only fairly sure of.

Nell remains in the office with the door open, pencil moving across the rota sheet. From upstairs comes the occasional small sound of Dev sorting equipment in the booth, nothing loud enough to disturb the work below.

You stand near the café tables with the glass cool in your hand. Beyond the front doors, Harbour Street has gone blue with evening, the harbour lights beginning to show at the end of the slope.

turns.input: If Owen is around and not busy, I ask whether he recommends any walks for a day off. Otherwise I leave him to his evening.
turns.output:
Owen is at the café counter, folding the bread tea towel while he waits for the board session to finish. You ask whether he recommends any walks for a day off.

He considers it. “Go north along the promenade, then take the steps by the old coastguard cottages. The cliff path takes you out to the signal hut. After that, turn inland behind the caravan site and come back past the football ground.”

He nods toward the darkening front doors. “It’s a couple of hours if you keep moving. Don’t come back along the beach unless you’ve checked the tide first.”

From the auditorium comes another camera shutter, followed by Rosa asking Martin for the spelling of a name. Owen glances at the clock, sets the folded tea towel on the counter, and remains nearby until it is time to help with the boards.

turns.input: I thank him if we have been talking, then go upstairs for the night. I do not press anyone for a longer conversation.
turns.output:
“Thanks,” you say.

Owen nods toward the front doors. “Watch the steps if it’s wet.”

You leave him at the counter and take the staff staircase upstairs. The projection booth door is shut on the landing; a low mechanical click sounds from within, then quiet.

In your room, the desk lamp throws a small circle of light across the welcome sheet and your luggage. Downstairs, the Picture House continues with its separate evening work while you close the door for the night.

turns.input: I sleep, have breakfast, and arrive for the nine o'clock induction on time. I let Nell begin.
turns.output:
After breakfast, you come downstairs a few minutes before nine. The supper tables have been cleared; only a faint smell of onion and washing-up liquid remains in the café. Nothing blocks the foyer now, and the auditorium doors are shut.

Nell is waiting in the office with a slim folder, a ring of keys, and a blue archive box tucked under one arm.

“Morning, Rowan. We’ll start upstairs.”

She leads the way to the first-floor landing and unlocks the archive workroom. Daylight lies flat across the folding tables. Shelves run along two walls, holding labelled programme boxes, files, and a small row of photograph cartons. At the far end stands the lockable cupboard.

Nell sets the folder and box on the nearest table. “The useful part of this job is making the collection intelligible to somebody who hasn’t been here. So every entry needs enough information for the next person to find the thing again and understand why we’ve described it that way.”

She opens the folder to a printed template.

“Object or group number. Description. Date, if we have one, and how we know it. Condition. Provenance. Ownership or loan status. Then restrictions, if there are any.”

Her finger moves down the columns.

“If a date comes from a printed programme, that’s one thing. If it comes from somebody’s recollection, record whose recollection it is. Don’t clean, repair, flatten, or split up a group of papers because it would look tidier. If something seems wrong, fragile, or uncertain, leave it where it is and bring me in.”

She looks toward the locked cupboard.

“That holds lent material. I keep the key. Bea Finch’s green photograph album is in there. We can inventory it and write condition descriptions under the loan record, but it is not to be scanned, copied, published, or put on display. If anyone asks to use images from it, they speak to Bea through me. The exhibition work downstairs doesn’t change that.”

Nell closes the folder and slides the blue box toward the middle of the table.

“This one is straightforward: old business material acquired with the cinema archive. Mixed programme bundles, mostly. We’ll do the first entry together, then you can work through the rest at a sensible pace.”

She lifts the lid. Inside, programmes lie in neat paper-wrapped groups, their edges softened by years of handling. Nell takes the top bundle without undoing its string and places a blank record sheet beside it.

turns.input: During the induction I ask how to tell what the cinema owns from what is on loan, and what restrictions I need to check before handling an item.
turns.output:
Nell opens the folder to two separate sections.

“Don’t decide from the object itself,” she says. “A programme about this cinema might be trust property, somebody’s donation, or something they’ve only lent us. Being old and cinema-related doesn’t settle it.”

She taps the blue box’s reference label, then an entry on the acquisition list. “For trust material, you match the box, bundle, or item to the transfer and acquisition records. This box came in with the old business archive, so that supports recording the trust as owner at group level. If a loose item doesn’t match a record, you don’t make a guess. Record what you can see, mark its status as unconfirmed, and put it aside for me.”

She turns to the loan register.

“For loans, the signed agreement tells us both whose it is and what we can do with it. Read that before you begin work, along with any label or note kept with the material. A loan isn’t automatically hands-off; it depends on the terms.”

Her hand rests briefly on the locked cupboard at the far end of the room.

“Bea’s photograph album can be inventoried and condition-described. It cannot be scanned, copied, published, or displayed without a further agreement from her. That remains true even if someone thinks a picture would be useful for the exhibition.”

Nell returns to the blank record sheet. “Before handling anything, check the record, look at its condition where it sits, and keep groups together unless we agree otherwise. Stable programmes can be handled gently for cataloguing. But no cleaning, repairs, flattening, or taking apart bundles to make them neater. If paper is brittle, damp, stuck, or unclear, you stop and flag it.”

She sets the acquisition entry beside the paper-wrapped bundle.

“The important thing is that someone reading your record can see what you know, where it came from, and what remains uncertain.”

turns.input: If the loaned photograph album is among the items explained to me, I ask whether one of its photographs could be displayed for the reopening. I do not copy, scan, or publish anything. Otherwise I ask about the permissions on whichever loaned item we are discussing.
turns.output:
Nell looks toward the locked cupboard.

“Not under the current agreement,” she says. “The album can be inventoried and condition-described. Displaying even one photograph needs Bea’s further written agreement first.”

She closes the loan register over the relevant page. “She wants to speak to some of the people pictured before deciding what can be public. If that ever changes, I’ll update the record. Until then, you note the restriction and leave the decision with her.”

Nell returns her attention to the blue box. “For this bundle, the acquisition record is enough to establish trust ownership. Shall we make the first entry together?”

turns.input: I accept the answer about permissions and work within it. I begin the cataloguing tasks I have actually been assigned.
turns.output:
You leave the loan register closed and the green album in its locked cupboard. The blue box on the table is a different case.

Nell lays its acquisition record beside the blank sheet. “This tells you why we can call it trust property,” she says, indicating the transfer schedule. “The programmes themselves can tell you dates and titles. Keep those sources separate.”

The first paper-wrapped bundle contains weekly programmes, still in their original order. Together, you record it as a group: printed programmes; dates taken from the covers; softened edges and creases, with the wrapper torn at one corner; transferred with the former cinema’s business archive; owned by the trust.

Nell has you note that the date range comes from the programmes themselves, rather than treating the acquisition paperwork as proof of when they were issued. She checks the completed entry, then slides the next bundle within reach.

“That’s the method,” she says. “Work steadily. If the order seems meaningful, preserve it. If something doesn’t match the records, stop and mark it for me.”

She takes the folder back to the office, leaving the archive workroom quiet around you.

You begin on the next bundle, keeping its wrapping and sequence intact as you describe what is there. The locked cupboard remains at the far end of the room, separate from the trust-owned material on the shelves.

turns.input: I work quietly through the rest of the morning, putting any loaned material away securely when I stop.
turns.output:
You work steadily through the morning, keeping each programme bundle in its existing order and recording dates only where the covers supply them. The entries accumulate: titles, date ranges, creased corners, torn wrappers, and the acquisition record that establishes the trust’s ownership.

The work stays with the blue box and its listed contents. You do not open the locked loan cupboard; Bea’s album remains secured there under its separate terms.

Near midday, you return the catalogued bundles to the box in their original sequence, leave the completed record sheets together on the table, and mark the next bundle for the afternoon.

turns.input: At lunch, if Bea is present, I ask what she enjoys about having the cinema open again. If she is not here, I eat with whoever is around.
turns.output:
Near half past twelve, you mark your place in the next bundle and go downstairs with your lunch.

Bea is at one of the café tables, a paper sandwich wrapper folded beside her mug. A slim folder rests against her bag. Nell stands at the office door, taking two invoices from it.

“Caught you,” Bea says to Nell. “I’m meant to be back at the boatyard before one.”

Nell tucks the papers beneath her clipboard. “I’ve got them. Thank you.”

Bea notices you and gestures to the chair opposite. “Sit down, Rowan. I was in and out yesterday before I properly said hello.”

You take the chair. Jo is working quietly in the kitchen, and the foyer has the spare, daytime feel of a place not yet open to customers.

“What do you enjoy about having the cinema open again?” you ask.

Bea considers that while she unscrews the lid from her coffee.

“Some of it’s very ordinary,” she says. “I like people making an evening of it. When I ushered here, there were always the same sorts: people arriving absurdly early, someone complaining about the adverts, children trying to get through the doors ahead of everyone else. You got to know the rhythm of a Friday.”

She looks through the front doors toward Harbour Street.

“At the boatyard, I see plenty of people on payroll I never see anywhere else. A cinema gets people out at the same time for something that isn’t a shift, or shopping, or a funeral reception.”

Then she gives a small shrug.

“I don’t want it preserved like a museum piece, mind. The old place had dreadful heating and worse toilets. I want it to work now. Good films, decent staff, a café that can stay open.” Her glance moves briefly toward the kitchen. “And somewhere nearby to watch the terrible discs my granddaughter sends me.”

The clock above the counter catches her eye. Bea folds the sandwich wrapper again and puts it into her bag.

“I’d better get back. Payroll is less forgiving than cinema work.”

She takes her folder’s empty sleeve, gives you a brief nod, and heads out into the brightening afternoon.

turns.input: I let the conversation finish and go back to the catalogue. I work until the end of my agreed shift.
turns.output:
You return to the archive workroom and continue through the programme bundles at a steady pace. Each group stays in its existing order; dates come from the printed covers, and condition notes distinguish creases and wear from anything that needs Nell’s attention.

By the end of your agreed shift, you have added several more completed records. You return the last bundle to the blue box in sequence, leave the sheets together for Nell, and mark where to resume tomorrow. The loan cupboard remains locked and undisturbed.

Your workday at the Picture House is over.

turns.input: The following morning I check with Nell for my next archive assignment and any practical changes I need to know about.
turns.output:
Wednesday morning, Nell is at her office desk with yesterday’s record sheets spread beside the rota clipboard.

You check in about the next archive task and whether anything has changed that affects your work.

She scans the completed entries first. “These are clear. You’ve kept the source of each date separate from the acquisition record, which is exactly what I need.”

She taps the blue box waiting on the archive-room table upstairs. “Finish that box this morning. When it’s done, bring me the sheets and I’ll file them with the acquisition paperwork.”

Then she lifts a grey records carton from the floor beside her desk. Its label reads *Business papers: suppliers and bookings*.

“This is next. It came with the former cinema archive, so the transfer schedule supports trust ownership, but it’s a mixed group. Invoices, correspondence, booking notes, some carbon copies. Keep its internal order as you find it, and don’t separate anything just because it looks untidy.”

“No practical changes to your hours or access today,” she adds. “The loan cupboard remains mine to unlock, and the same restrictions apply if we get to any lent material later.”

She gathers the rota sheets into a neater stack. “If you find something that seems to belong somewhere else, flag it before moving it. Otherwise, carry on.”

Upstairs, the archive workroom is cool and still. The programme box waits where you left it, your marked bundle near the top. The grey carton remains downstairs for later, its practical, unglamorous papers promising a different sort of history once the morning’s programmes are complete.

turns.input: I say I am not available for additional front-of-house shifts; I want to keep the hours outside my archive contract for myself.
turns.output:
Before taking the next box upstairs, you tell Nell that you are not available for extra front-of-house shifts and intend to keep time outside your archive contract for yourself.

“That’s fine,” she says plainly. “You’re here for the archive work, thirty hours a week. I haven’t put you on the front-of-house rota.”

She squares the stack of completed sheets on her desk. “If something outside that ever comes up, I’ll ask. I won’t treat your evenings as assumed availability.”

With that settled, she indicates the programme box upstairs. “Finish that first. Then we’ll look at the business-papers carton.”

turns.input: If Owen is around during a break, I ask how his week is going. If he is not, I take my break without looking for him.
turns.output:
During your break, Owen is at the café counter sorting opening programmes into small stacks. He looks up when you ask how his week is going.

“Not bad,” he says. “Busy, but that was always going to be the case.” He squares one pile against the counter. “There’s something satisfying about getting a place ready before anyone starts asking where the toilets are.”

He glances toward the auditorium doors.

“Your archive work settling in all right?”

turns.input: If we have been talking, I tell Owen I will see him tomorrow. Then I take a walk along the harbour on my own.
turns.output:
“I’ll see you tomorrow,” you tell Owen.

“Yeah. See you,” he says, returning to the programme stacks.

You leave by the front doors and head downhill along Harbour Street toward the water. The harbour is busy in its quiet daytime way: ropes knock against masts, a gull worries at something near the fish-market bins, and two men in waterproof trousers work over a boat’s open engine hatch.

You follow the wall beside the inner harbour, past the chipped blue railings and the row of nets drying on hooks. The air smells of salt, diesel, and seaweed caught below the tide line. Across the water, the pale fronts of the seafront hotels sit under a broad, bright sky.

For a while, nobody from the Picture House needs anything from you.
